system_prompt:
You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'. Keep explanations short (under 6-8 words per term).
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. CONCISENESS & LENGTH CONSTRAINT (CRITICAL): The simplified text must be concise and proportionate, strictly between 1.2x and 2.0x the word length of the original source report. Do NOT over-expand. Never list hypothetical normal ranges or unmentioned medical conditions. Only mention normal ranges for tests/vitals explicitly recorded in the document.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and brief purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic to fight infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (machine filtering waste when kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.

On arrival, his temperature was 99.8°F (mild fever), pulse was 112 bpm (fast heart rate; normal is 60–100), blood pressure was 100/70 mmHg (borderline low; normal is 120/80), respiratory rate was 20/min, and oxygen was normal at 98%. Blood tests showed leukocytosis (mild rise in infection-fighting cells) and hyponatremia (low salt/sodium levels due to fluid loss). Stool tests showed no blood or parasites. You were admitted on 11/08/2020 and discharged on 01/02/2021 after a stay of 1 m 24 d 15 h in the ward (payer: sus). You came for severe left lower back pain that started 3 days earlier, along with weakness (asthenia) and difficulty walking. You did not have fever, nausea or vomiting. The dressing of the Schilley catheter (central line) in the right femoral vein was leaking.

During the hospital stay you were diagnosed with several infections. Blood cultures on 11/08 showed staphylococcus aureus MRSA (a resistant bacteria) and the catheter tip also grew the same organism, so the catheter was removed on 11/08. Vancomycin (an antibiotic to fight resistant bacteria) was started on 11/08 and continued after each dialysis session. Later cultures on 11/11, 11/21, 11/24 grew other bacteria (oxa‑resistant staphylococcus, citrobacter koseri, staphylococcus capitis) but from 11/28 to 12/02 all blood cultures were negative, and you remained without fever.

Imaging showed a vegetation (infection growth) on the mitral valve (heart valve) on an echocardiogram performed on 11/18, confirming bacterial endocarditis (infection of the heart lining). A CT scan of the lumbosacral spine on 11/12 suggested a fracture of the L1 vertebral body due to bone fragility, gas in the spinal canal at L2‑L3 that could be from a disc herniation, and an infectious or inflammatory process that could not be ruled out. An MRI on 25/11/2020 showed infectious spondylodiscitis (infection of the spine bones and discs) at L3‑L4 with an anterior epidural abscess (pus collection in front of the spinal cord). Another MRI on 25/10/2020 revealed a left iliopsoas abscess (pus collection in a deep thigh muscle) measuring 15 × 2.1 × 1.8 cm with surrounding swelling (edema) and contrast enhancement. An attempt on 12/02 by {organization} to drain this abscess percutaneously (through the skin) was not done because bowel loops were in the way.

Because you could not move much, a sacral pressure injury (bed sore) developed. It was treated with surgical debridement (removal of dead tissue) and local wound care, and the team gave you written instructions for home care. Your left upper‑limb arteriovenous fistula (surgical connection for dialysis) was functional but showed narrowing (stenosis). You continue to need hemodialysis (machine cleaning of blood) on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays. A phlebography (X‑ray of the fistula) is planned to locate the narrowing and decide on further treatment.

On examination at discharge you were in good general condition: pale (1/4), hydrated, without cyanosis (no blue skin), without jaundice, afebrile to the touch and breathing comfortably in room air. You were alert and oriented to time, place and person. Lung sounds were normal with faint crackles at the bases, but you had no breathing difficulty. Heart rhythm was irregular but sounds were normal and there were no murmurs. The abdomen was soft, slightly swollen, with normal bowel sounds, not tender and no signs of peritoneal irritation. Your limbs were warm and well perfused. The left arm showed a palpable thrill (vibration) over the fistula, indicating flow. The lower limbs had mild swelling and a small area of yellowish skin change (anterior tibial ochre dermatitis).

Your medication list from before admission was continued, and vancomycin 0.5 g is to be given after each scheduled dialysis session until 01/09/2021, completing six weeks after the last negative blood culture. You are to have a phlebography of the arteriovenous fistula (brachial approach) to assess the stenosis, with ultrasound guidance if needed. The sacral pressure injury clinic will see you on 16/01/2021 for reassessment, and you have been given home‑care instructions for the wound. Cardiology will follow you for amyloidosis investigation; the appointment missed on 09/09 will be rescheduled, and a new visit is planned for 01/13. Motor rehabilitation was scheduled for 01/13, and you are awaiting a physiatry appointment requested on 12/27. The pelvis MRI report from 12/16 should be reviewed. You will continue dialysis on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays at the unit of {organization}, with transport provided by stretcher taxi {omitted}. All these plans were recorded in the discharge note.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'. Keep explanations short (under 6-8 words per term).
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. CONCISENESS & LENGTH CONSTRAINT (CRITICAL): The simplified text must be concise and proportionate, strictly between 1.2x and 2.0x the word length of the original source report. Do NOT over-expand. Never list hypothetical normal ranges or unmentioned medical conditions. Only mention normal ranges for tests/vitals explicitly recorded in the document.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.

If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and brief purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic to fight infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (machine filtering waste when kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.

output_text:
You were admitted on 11/08/2020 because the dressing of the Schilley catheter (tube placed in a vein) in the right femoral vein (groin vein) was leaking and you had severe left lower back pain that started three days earlier, along with weakness (asthenia) and difficulty walking. You did not have fever, nausea, vomiting or any other symptoms, and the person who came with you said the same.

During the hospital stay, doctors found several serious infections. A blood test showed a bloodstream infection (infection in the blood) caused by Staphylococcus aureus MRSA (a type of “super‑bug”). The same bug was also found on the catheter tip on 11/08. Because of this, the catheter was removed on 11/08 and you started an antibiotic called vancomycin (a medicine that fights serious bacterial infections) on the same day, guided by the lab results. Your blood cultures became negative after a few days and you stayed without fever (afebrile) for the rest of the stay.

Imaging of your spine showed pyogenic spondylodiscitis (bone infection) at the L3‑L4 levels, which explained the low back pain and the trouble walking. A CT scan (special X‑ray) on 11/12 showed a fracture of the L1 vertebral body (spine bone) because the bone was weak, and gas pockets in the spinal canal at L2‑L3 that could be from a slipped disc (extruded disc herniation) with wear‑and‑tear changes (degenerative disc disease). An MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) on 25/11/2020 confirmed infectious spondylodiscitis with an anterior epidural abscess (pus collection in front of the spinal cord). Another MRI of the pelvis on 25/10/2020 showed a left ileopsoas abscess (pus collection in a deep muscle of the abdomen) measuring 15 × 2.1 × 1.8 cm with swelling (edema) and contrast enhancement. A percutaneous drainage attempt (needle drainage through the skin) on 12/02 was not done because loops of bowel were in the way, as noted by {organization}.

An echocardiogram (ultrasound of the heart) done on 11/18 revealed bacterial endocarditis (infection of the heart lining) with a vegetation (small growth) on the mitral valve (one of the heart’s doors). This was also linked to the same Staphylococcus aureus infection.

Because you could not move much, you developed a sacral pressure injury (bed sore on the lower back). This was treated with surgical debridement (removal of dead tissue) and local wound care, and the wound‑care instructions were given to you.

You also needed regular hemodialysis (machine that cleans the blood) on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays because of an arteriovenous fistula (a surgically created connection in the left upper arm to help dialysis). The fistula showed narrowing (stenosis) that will be evaluated later with a vein X‑ray (phlebography) and possibly an ultrasound.

At discharge on 01/02/2021, after a stay of 1 month 24 days 15 hours, you were in good general condition: you looked a little pale (about one‑quarter pale), were hydrated, had normal skin colour (acyanic, anicteric), no fever to the touch, and breathed comfortably in room air. You were awake, aware of time, place and person. Your lungs made normal breath sounds with a few faint crackles at the bases but no breathing trouble. Your heart rhythm was irregular but the sounds were normal and there were no murmurs. Your abdomen was slightly swollen but soft, with normal bowel sounds, normal blood pressure (normotensive), and no pain on pressing. Your arms were warm with good blood flow; the left arm showed a palpable thrill (vibration) over the fistula. Your legs had mild swelling and a yellowish skin change on the front of the lower leg (anterior tibial ochre dermatitis).

The lab results during the stay were: catheter tip culture on 11/08 showed vancomycin‑sensitive Staphylococcus aureus; blood cultures on 11/08, 11/11, 11/21, 11/24 showed Staphylococcus aureus (some resistant to oxacillin) and one sample with Citrobacter koseri; a culture on 11/28 was negative, as were cultures on 12/01 and 12/02.

The plan after discharge includes giving 0.5 g of vancomycin after each scheduled hemodialysis session, continuing the antibiotic until 01/09/2021, which will be six weeks after the last negative blood culture. You will have a phlebography (vein X‑ray) of the arteriovenous fistula to locate the narrowing and decide on further treatment; this may be done with ultrasound guidance in the dialysis room. You are on the waiting list for this test, and {organization} will contact you to arrange it.

You have several follow‑up appointments: an outpatient visit on 16/01/2021 to check the sacral pressure injury and receive home‑care instructions; a cardiology outpatient visit for amyloidosis (protein deposit disease of the heart) investigation on 01/13; a motor‑rehabilitation appointment that was missed on 09/09 and is now scheduled for 01/13; and a physiatry (rehab medicine) appointment requested on 12/27. You should also review the pelvic MRI report from 12/16. Your previous chronic medicines will be continued, and you will keep attending dialysis on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays.

Please keep the transportation arrangement (stretcher taxi) {omitted} for your trips to the dialysis unit, and follow all the wound‑care and medication instructions given by the team.

Here are examples of what I expect:

--- Example 1 ---
Original Medical Report:
Patient Name: Michael Smith | Age/Sex: 32/M | Admission: 02/03/2026 | Discharge: 05/03/2026
C/O: Loose stools, vomiting, and abdominal cramps for 3 days.
History: Multiple episodes of watery diarrhea with nausea, repeated vomiting, generalised weakness, and abdominal cramps. No blood in stools. No recent travel.
Past History: Hypothyroidism (2 years).
Examination: Temp 99.8°F | Pulse 112 bpm | BP 100/70 mmHg | RR 20/min | SpO₂ 98%.
Investigations: CBC — mild leukocytosis. Serum Electrolytes — hyponatremia. Stool — no blood/parasites. RFT — mildly elevated creatinine due to dehydration.

Output:
Michael Smith, a 32-year-old man, was admitted on 02/03/2026 and discharged on 05/03/2026. He came with 3 days of loose motions (watery diarrhea), vomiting, stomach cramps, and weakness. He has had hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid) for 2 years. On arrival, his temperature was 99.8°F (mild fever), pulse was 112 bpm (fast heart rate; normal is 60–100), blood pressure was 100/70 mmHg (borderline low; normal is 120/80), respiratory rate was 20/min, and oxygen was normal at 98%. Blood tests showed leukocytosis (mild rise in infection-fighting cells) and hyponatremia (low salt/sodium levels due to fluid loss). Stool tests showed no blood or parasites. Kidney tests showed mildly raised creatinine due to dehydration (lack of fluids). He was treated with IV fluids and supportive medicines, improved well, and was safely discharged home.

--- Example 2 ---
Original Medical Report:
Patient Name: Robert Brown | Age/Sex: 58/M | Admission: 25/03/2026 | Discharge: 30/03/2026
C/O: Chest pain and sweating for 6 hours.
History: Sudden onset retrosternal chest pain radiating to the left arm, sweating, mild breathlessness.
Past History: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (8 years). Hypertension (10 years). Dyslipidemia.
Examination: Temp 98.4°F | Pulse 96 bpm | BP 160/100 mmHg | RR 22/min | SpO₂ 95%.
Investigations: ECG — ST depression in anterior leads. Troponin-I — elevated. 2D Echo — mild left ventricular dysfunction. Lipid Profile — elevated LDL cholesterol.

Output:
Robert Brown, a 58-year-old man, was admitted on 25/03/2026 and discharged on 30/03/2026. He has an 8-year history of diabetes (sugar), 10-year hypertension (high BP), and dyslipidemia (high blood cholesterol). He arrived with 6 hours of sudden central chest pain spreading to his left arm, sweating, and mild breathlessness. His temperature was 98.4°F (normal), pulse was 96 bpm, blood pressure was high at 160/100 mmHg (normal 120/80), and oxygen saturation was 95% (borderline). An ECG and elevated troponin-I (a heart damage marker) confirmed a mild heart attack. A 2D Echo (heart ultrasound scan) showed mild left ventricular dysfunction (mild pumping weakness of the heart), and tests showed elevated bad LDL cholesterol. He was stabilized on heart medications and blood thinners, recovered safely, and was discharged home.

The main problem found was a serious infection in the blood (bloodstream infection) caused by a resistant type of bacteria called Staphylococcus Aureus (MRSA). His kidneys are not working well (Chronic Kidney Disease), so he needs hemodialysis (a machine that cleans the blood) three times a week. There is also a narrowing (stenosis) in his arteriovenous fistula (the special blood vessel connection used for dialysis) in his left arm. Doctors also suspect he has amyloidosis (a condition where abnormal proteins build up in organs).

His blood cultures (tests to check for bacteria in the blood) became negative, meaning the infection in the blood is clearing up. The main problem was a bloodstream infection (infection in the blood) linked to a Schilley catheter (a tube for dialysis) in the right femoral vein (large vein in the thigh). This led to bacterial endocarditis (infection of the heart valve), specifically with vegetation (clot of bacteria) on the mitral valve, as seen on an echocardiogram (heart ultrasound) on 11/18. There was also pyogenic spondylodiscitis (infection of the spine and discs) at the L3/L4 level, causing low back pain and gait disturbance (difficulty walking). A CT scan (X-ray scan) of the lumbosacral spine on 11/12 showed a fracture due to bone fragility at L1, gas in the spinal canal at L2/L3 possibly from a disc herniation (disc slipping out), and possible infection. An MRI (magnetic scan) on 25/11/2020 confirmed infectious spondylodiscitis with an anterior epidural abscess (pus collection near the spine). Additionally, an MRI on 25/10/2020 showed a left ileopsoas abscess (pus pocket in the hip muscle) measuring 15 x 2.1 x 1.8 cm.

[person] came in with severe left lower back pain, weakness, and altered gait, but no fever, nausea, or vomiting. The catheter dressing was leaking. During the stay, the infection was identified as Staphylococcus aureus MRSA (a type of resistant bacteria). The catheter was removed on 11/08, and antibiotic therapy with Vancomycin (an antibiotic) was started. An attempt to drain the psoas abscess percutaneously (through the skin) on 12/02 was not done because bowel loops (intestines) were in the way. Imaging showed improvement in the spine infections, so conservative treatment (non-surgical care) was continued. [person] remained afebrile (no fever) with negative blood cultures. Due to immobility, a sacral pressure injury (bed sore on the tailbone) developed, which was treated with surgical debridement (cleaning of dead tissue) and local care. [person] requires hemodialysis (machine filtering waste from blood) on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays using an arteriovenous fistula (surgical connection for dialysis) in the left arm, though a local stenosis (narrowing) was noted.

On examination, [person] is in good general condition, pale, hydrated, and breathing normally on room air. He is conscious and oriented. Breath sounds are clear with slight crackles at the bases. Heart rhythm is irregular but sounds are normal with no murmurs. The abdomen is soft and painless. Limbs are warm and well-perfused (good blood flow). The left arm fistula has a thrill (vibration from blood flow). There is slight swelling and skin changes on the lower legs. Cultures showed Vancomycin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus initially, followed by Citrobacter koseri and Staphylococcus capitis, with negative cultures from 11/28 onwards.

For discharge, [person] must take 0.5 g of Vancomycin after each hemodialysis session until 01/09/2021, completing 6 weeks after the last negative blood culture. You also felt very weak (asthenia) and had difficulty walking (altered gait). The person with you said you did not have fever, nausea (feeling like vomiting), or vomiting, or any other related symptoms. We noticed that the dressing on the special tube (Schilley catheter) in your right groin area (femoral vein sac) was leaking.

During your time in the hospital, we found that you had a bloodstream infection (an infection in your blood) caused by a type of bacteria called Staphylococcus aureus MRSA (a specific kind of bacteria that is resistant to some common antibiotics). This infection led to a few other problems:

1.  **Infection in your spine:** You had pyogenic spondylodiscitis (a serious infection of the bones and discs in your spine) in your L3/L4 vertebrae (bones in your lower back). This was causing your low back pain and difficulty walking. A CT scan (a special X-ray that takes detailed pictures) of your lower back (lumbosacral spine) on 11/12 showed signs of a fracture (a break) in your L1 vertebra (another bone in your lower back) due to bone fragility (weak bones). It also showed some gas pockets in your spinal canal (the space inside your spine where nerves are) at the L2/L3 level, which might be related to a slipped disc (extruded disc herniation) and wear and tear of your discs (degenerative disc disease). We couldn't rule out an infection or inflammation there either. Later, an MRI (a more detailed scan using magnets) of your lower back on 25/11/2020 confirmed an infectious spondylodiscitis (spinal infection) with an anterior epidural abscess (a collection of pus in front of the spinal cord).
2.  **Heart infection:** You also developed bacterial endocarditis (an infection of the inner lining of your heart, usually affecting the valves) which was linked to the catheter. An echocardiogram (an ultrasound scan of your heart) on 11/18 showed a growth (vegetation) on your mitral valve (one of the heart valves).
3.  **Abscess in your muscle:** You had a left ileopsoas abscess (a collection of pus in a muscle deep in your abdomen and hip). An MRI on 25/10/2020 showed this collection of pus (intramuscular collection) in your left ileopsoas muscle, measuring 15 x 2.1 x 1.8 cm, with swelling (edema) and signs of inflammation after a special dye was given (post-contrast enhancement).

output_text:
Your family member was admitted on 11/08/2020 and discharged on 01/02/2021, staying for 1 month, 24 days, and 15 hours.

He came to the hospital for a hemodialysis (blood filtering machine for kidney failure) session with severe left lower back pain that had started 3 days ago, along with weakness and difficulty walking. The person accompanying him said he did not have fever, nausea, or vomiting. The catheter (a tube for dialysis) dressing in his right thigh vein was leaking.

During his hospital stay, he was diagnosed with several serious infections. He had a bloodstream infection (infection in the blood) caused by Staphylococcus aureus MRSA (a type of bacteria resistant to some antibiotics). This infection led to spondylodiscitis (infection of the spinal bones and discs) in his L2-L4 region (lower back), infective endocarditis (infection of the heart valve) in his mitral valve (one of the heart's main valves), and an ileopsoas muscle abscess (a collection of pus in a muscle near the hip) on the left side.

The catheter in his right thigh vein was removed on 11/08, and he was started on antibiotic therapy (treatment with medicines to fight infection) with vancomycin (a strong antibiotic) on the same day, based on culture (lab test to identify bacteria) results. An attempt to drain the abscess in his psoas muscle (a deep muscle in the abdomen) on 12/02 was not successful because bowel loops (parts of the intestine) were in the way.

He showed improvement in the infections in his spine with conservative treatment (treatment without surgery). He remained without fever, and his blood cultures (blood tests for infection) became negative repeatedly. As a complication of being immobile (not moving much), he developed a sacral pressure injury (a bed sore on the lower back), which was treated with surgical debridement (removal of dead tissue) and local care. Instructions for caring for this injury at home were given to the team.

He continued to need hemodialysis on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays because of a problem with his arteriovenous fistula (a surgically created connection between an artery and a vein for dialysis) in his left arm, where there was some narrowing. He is currently on renal replacement therapy (treatment for kidney failure, like dialysis).

His general condition is good. He is a bit pale, hydrated (has enough fluids), not blue (acyanotic), not jaundiced (anicteric), not feverish to the touch, and breathing normally (eupneic) in room air. Neurologically, he is conscious and knows where he is, what time it is, and who he is. When listening to his chest, there were normal breathing sounds with some mild crackles (small popping sounds) at the bottom of both lungs, but no signs of breathing difficulty. His heart rhythm was irregular, with normal heart sounds and no murmurs (abnormal heart sounds). His abdomen (belly) is slightly bulging, with normal bowel sounds, not tense, and not painful when touched lightly or deeply. His hands and feet are warm and have good blood flow. In his left arm, the fistula has a thrill (a vibration felt over the fistula, which is a good sign). In his legs, there is some mild swelling and a skin condition called anterior tibial ochre dermatitis (skin discoloration on the shins).

An MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) scan on 25/10/2020 showed a collection of pus in his left ileopsoas muscle, measuring 15 x 2.1 x 1.8 cm, with swelling and enhancement (brightening on the scan after dye injection).

Culture results showed:
- Catheter tip on 11/08: Staphylococcus aureus sensitive to vancomycin.
- Blood culture on 11/08: Staphylococcus aureus.
- Blood culture on 11/11: Staphylococcus aureus resistant to oxacillin (another antibiotic) in 2 samples.
- Blood culture on 11/21: Citrobacter koseri (another type of bacteria) in 1 sample, and Staphylococcus aureus in 1 sample.
- Blood culture on 11/24: Staphylococcus capitis (another type of bacteria).
- Blood cultures on 11/28, 12/01, and 12/02 were negative.

An attempted puncture to drain the abscess on 12/02 was not done because of intestinal loops being in the way. A new MRI report of the pelvis from 12/16 was reviewed.

It has been arranged with {organization} for him to attend hemodialysis at {organization} on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays, with transport by stretcher taxi from his home city.

Therefore, he is being discharged with the following pending issues:
- He needs to be given 0.5 grams of vancomycin after each scheduled hemodialysis session. This antibiotic treatment will continue until 01/09/2021, completing 6 weeks after his last negative blood culture.
- His arteriovenous fistula needs assessment. A phlebography (X-ray of veins with dye) of the fistula is recommended to find the site of narrowing, or an ultrasound can be done before the procedure. He has been put on a list for this, and {organization} will contact him to schedule the treatment.
- For the sacral pressure injury, the specialist team has noted that he has an outpatient follow-up appointment on 16/01/2021 for reassessment. Instructions for home care of the injury were provided.
- For cardiology (heart specialist) follow-up to investigate amyloidosis (a condition where abnormal protein builds up in organs), he missed an appointment on 09/09. A new appointment is scheduled for 01/13.
- For motor rehabilitation (therapy to improve movement), an appointment with the physiatry department (physical medicine and rehabilitation) at {organization} was requested on 12/27, and we are awaiting the appointment.
- The nuclear magnetic resonance report of the pelvis from 12/16 needs to be checked.
- His previous chronic medications (long-term medicines) are to be continued.
- He will go to the dialysis room on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays.
- He has an appointment at the amyloidosis cardiology outpatient clinic on 01/13.
- He has an appointment at the pressure injury surgery outpatient clinic on 01/16.

You were admitted to the hospital on November 8, 2020, and discharged on February 1, 2021, after staying for 1 month, 24 days, and 15 hours.

When you came to the hospital, you were having severe pain in your lower left back that had started three days earlier. You also felt weak (asthenia) and had trouble walking (altered gait). The person with you said you did not have fever, nausea (feeling like vomiting), or vomiting. The dressing on your catheter (a tube inserted into your body) in your right thigh vein (femoral vein) was leaking.

During your hospital stay, doctors found you had a bloodstream infection (infection in your blood) caused by a bacteria called Staphylococcus aureus MRSA. This infection led to several other problems:

1.  **Bloodstream infection:** This was linked to a Schilley catheter (a type of tube) in your right thigh vein.
2.  **Bacterial endocarditis:** This is an infection of the inner lining of your heart. An echocardiogram (a heart ultrasound) on November 18 showed a growth (vegetation) on your mitral valve (one of your heart valves).
3.  **Pyogenic spondylodiscitis:** This is a bacterial infection of your spinal bones (vertebrae) and the discs between them, specifically at your L3/L4 level (lower back). On November 5, you had low back pain and trouble walking. A CT scan (a special X-ray) of your lower back on November 12 showed signs of a fracture (a break) in your L1 spinal bone due to weak bones (bone fragility). It also showed gas in your spinal canal at the L2/L3 level, which might be from a slipped disc (extruded disc herniation) with wear and tear of the discs (degenerative disc disease). An infection or inflammation could not be ruled out. Later, an MRI (a detailed scan) of your lower back on November 25, 2020, confirmed an infectious spondylodiscitis with an abscess (a collection of pus) in front of your spinal cord (anterior epidural abscess).
4.  **Left ileopsoas abscess:** This is a collection of pus in your left ileopsoas muscle (a muscle in your hip). An MRI on October 25, 2020, showed a collection of fluid in this muscle, measuring 15 x 2.1 x 1.8 cm, with swelling (edema) and enhancement after a special dye was given.

Your catheter was removed on November 8, and you were started on an antibiotic (medicine to fight infection) called Vancomycin, based on culture results (tests to identify the bacteria). An attempt was made on December 2 by {organization} to drain the abscess in your psoas muscle (percutaneous drainage), but it could not be done because your intestines (bowel loops) were in the way.

Doctors observed that the problems in your spine (axial lesions) showed improvement on scans, and you continued to receive conservative treatment (treatment without surgery) for the infections found during your stay. You did not have a fever (remained afebrile), and your blood cultures (tests for infection in blood) repeatedly came back negative.

As a complication from not moving much, you developed a sacral pressure injury (a bedsore on your lower back). This was treated with surgical debridement (removing dead tissue) and other local treatments. The team gave you instructions on how to care for this injury at home.

You also needed hemodialysis (a machine filtering waste when kidneys cannot) on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays because of a problem with your arteriovenous fistula (a connection made between an artery and a vein for dialysis) in your left arm. There was a narrowing (stenosis) in it. You are currently on renal replacement therapy (treatment for kidney failure).

Your general condition is good. You are a bit pale, well-hydrated, not blue (acyanotic), not jaundiced (anicteric), not feverish to the touch, and breathing normally (eupneic) in room air. Your brain function (neurology) is normal; you are conscious and know the time, place, and who you are. Your lungs sound clear with some minor crackling sounds at the bottom, and you are not having trouble breathing. Your heart rhythm is irregular, but the sounds are normal, with no murmurs (abnormal heart sounds). Your abdomen (tummy) is slightly bulging, with normal bowel sounds, not tense, and not painful when touched lightly or deeply. Your hands and feet are warm and have good blood flow. In your left arm, the fistula has a normal vibration (thrill). Your legs have slight swelling (edema) and some brownish skin discoloration (anterior tibial ochre dermatitis) on the front of your shins.

Cultures (tests for bacteria) showed:
*   Catheter tip on November 8: Staphylococcus aureus, sensitive to Vancomycin.
*   Blood culture on November 8: Staphylococcus aureus.
*   Blood culture on November 11: Staphylococcus aureus, resistant to Oxacillin (oxa r) in two samples.
*   Blood culture on November 21: Citrobacter koseri in one sample, Staphylococcus aureus in one sample.
*   Blood culture on November 24: Staphylococcus capitis.
*   Blood cultures on November 28, December 1, and December 2 were all negative.

An MRI of your pelvis was done on December 16. It has been arranged with [organization] for you to attend hemodialysis at [organization] on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays. Transportation from your home city to the unit will be by stretcher taxi.

You are being discharged with the following instructions and pending issues:

*   **Medication:** You need to take 0.5 grams of Vancomycin after each scheduled hemodialysis session. This antibiotic treatment will continue until January 9, 2021, completing 6 weeks after your last negative blood culture.
*   **Arteriovenous fistula assessment:** You need a phlebography (a special X-ray of veins) of your fistula to find out where the narrowing (stenosis) is. This will help decide if another phlebography or an ultrasound before the procedure is needed. You have been put on a list, and [organization] will contact you to schedule this.
*   **Sacral pressure injury:** The specialist team for your pressure injury noted that your follow-up appointment is on January 16, 2021, for reassessment. You have been given instructions for home care of the injury.
*   **Cardiology follow-up:** You need to follow up with a heart doctor (cardiologist) to investigate amyloidosis (a condition where abnormal protein builds up in organs). You missed an appointment on September 9, and a new one is scheduled for January 13.
*   **Motor rehabilitation:** You need an appointment with the physiatry department (physical medicine and rehabilitation) at [organization] for motor rehabilitation (therapy to improve movement). This was requested on December 27, and we are waiting for the appointment.
*   **MRI report:** The nuclear magnetic resonance (MRI) report of your pelvis from December 16 needs to be checked.
*   **Chronic medications:** Your previous long-term medications will be continued.

Your main diagnosis is Sensitive Pulmonary Tuberculosis (TB in the lungs), which was first diagnosed in 2019. You also developed several serious complications related to this TB. These include a spontaneous pneumothorax (air leaking into the space around the right lung), lung collapse, a surgical wound infection caused by a tough bacteria called Multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, hypovolemic shock (a dangerous drop in blood volume due to bleeding from the surgical site), and a cardiopulmonary arrest (a temporary stop of the heart and breathing) that occurred on 10/04 due to low oxygen levels.

When you were admitted, you had been suffering from a persistent dry cough for 4 weeks, night sweats, and a fever that was not measured. You also experienced shortness of breath (dyspnea) and, one day before admission, sudden pain in your right chest that spread to your neck, along with worsening breathlessness. You had also lost about 8 kg in weight over the previous month. Your general condition was noted as pale 1/4 (mildly pale, which is not the normal skin color), but you were hydrated and conscious. Your heart rate was 85 beats per minute, which is within the normal range of 60 to 100 beats per minute. Your oxygen saturation was 98%, which is within the normal range of 95-100%. However, your respiratory exam showed abolished breath sounds in the right hemithorax (no air movement heard in the right lung), whereas normal breath sounds should be heard in both lungs. A sputum test called Bacilloscopy (Ziehl-Neelsen) came back positive, showing 10 to 99 TB bacteria in 100 fields, while a normal result would be negative (0 bacilli). You were admitted on 09/19/2022 and discharged on 10/19/2022 after a stay of 1 month 11 hours in the ward. You are a 60‑year‑old woman, incomplete high‑school education, working as a cleaner, weighing about 60 kg (estimated) and 57 kg (predicted), height 164 cm.  

During this admission you had several serious problems: a resolved septic shock (dangerous infection causing very low blood pressure) with a pulmonary focus (lung infection), acute respiratory failure (severe breathing difficulty), hypotension (low BP), decreased level of consciousness (drowsy), a blood culture that grew staphylococcus aureus (type of bacteria) resistant to oxacillin (antibiotic), a coronavirus infection in March confirmed by RTPCR on 03/15, acute kidney injury (kidney damage) KDIGO 1 that resolved and was pre‑renal (due to low blood flow), and liver cirrhosis (scarring of the liver) with pleural effusion (fluid around the lung) that needed repeated thoracentesis (draining fluid from the chest) and paracentesis (draining fluid from the abdomen).  

On 09/19 a blood gas showed a pH of 7.378, albumin 0.49 g/dL, serum albumin 2.1 g/dL, glucose 164 mg/dL, LDH 72 U/L, and a thoracentesis yielded transudate (fluid low in protein) with protein 2 g/dL, serum protein 7.7 g/dL, LDH 72 U/L, serum LDH 279 U/L, pH 7.378, albumin 0.61 g/dL, serum albumin 1.9 g/dL, amylase 117 U/L, glucose 183 mg/dL and a gram‑stain negative culture. On 09/23 you had 700 mL of transudate drained, on 10/06 1000 mL, on 10/10 another 1000 mL and on 10/15 a further 1000 mL were removed.  

Your liver cirrhosis aetiology (cause) is still to be clarified in a follow‑up gastroclinic appointment. On 02/09/2022 you were advised to increase furosemide (diuretic that removes fluid) to 40 mg twice daily and spironolactone (potassium‑sparing diuretic) to 50 mg daily because of massive ascites (abdominal fluid), dyspnea (shortness of breath) and weight gain. A paracentesis that day removed 4.1 L of ascitic fluid, and another on 13/09 removed 1.4 L.  

You were referred from the emergency unit with a report of admission on 18/09/2022, 85 % room‑air oxygen saturation, obtunded (very sleepy), peripheral cyanosis (bluish skin) and livedo reticularis (mottled skin), and you were intubated (tube placed in the airway) without complications. Four ampoules of furosemide were given before transport but no urine was produced. You were admitted intubated, sedated with midazolam (calm‑inducing drug) and fentanyl (painkiller), paralyzed with rocuronium (muscle relaxant), and supported with norepinephrine (drug to raise BP) at 20 mL/h.  

Initially you were thought to have acute respiratory failure due to coronavirus, congestion or sepsis of pulmonary focus. Empirical ceftriaxone (antibiotic) was started and a diagnostic paracentesis showed no spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (infection of abdominal fluid). On the same day a thoracentesis removed 1000 mL of transudate and a relief paracentesis removed 4000 mL; albumin (protein given intravenously) was given because of the large fluid removal. A point‑of‑care ultrasound on 09/19 showed lung lines and pleural thickening, supporting the lung infection hypothesis.  

Because the blood culture grew staphylococcus aureus, clarithromycin (antibiotic) and clindamycin (antibiotic) were added on 09/24, and the regimen was changed from ceftriaxone + clarithromycin to levofloxacin (antibiotic) + oxacillin (antibiotic) as directed by the consulting team. An echocardiogram (heart ultrasound) was ordered to look for endocarditis (infection of the heart lining). On the morning of 09/27, antibiotics were escalated to meropenem (broad‑spectrum antibiotic) + oxacillin because CRP (inflammation marker) rose and more vasoactive drugs were needed.  

Your breathing improved, you were taken off the ventilator (extubated) on 10/03 and stopped supplemental oxygen on 10/13. The septic condition resolved and the antibiotic course finished on 10/08. You remained in hospital for 24‑hour nursing care, pressure‑injury (skin sore) management, oxygen therapy, and ongoing control of ascites and pleural effusion, as you had no social support for discharge.  

Your past liver history includes first diagnosis of cirrhosis with unclear cause, Child‑B7 MELD 9 (liver severity scores), biopsies in 07/2020 showing grade I fibrosis (early scarring) and in 2021 showing intense fibrosis with moderate steatosis (fatty liver) consistent with grade 2 steatohepatitis stage 3. Complications have been ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, upper gastrointestinal bleeding, and esophageal varices (enlarged veins in the esophagus) without recent bleeding.  

Other past conditions: diabetes mellitus (sugar disease) diagnosed 15 years ago, systemic arterial hypertension (high BP) for 10 years, non‑toxic multinodular goiter (enlarged thyroid) diagnosed 201

You were admitted on 09/19/2022 and discharged on 10/19/2022 after staying for 1 month 11 hours in a ward, with payment through SUS. You are a 60‑year‑old female, living at [address], with incomplete high school education and working as a cleaner. Your estimated weight was 60 kg, predicted weight 57 kg, and height 164 cm.

During this stay you had several serious problems. You had a resolved septic shock (dangerous infection causing low blood pressure) that started in the lungs (pulmonary focus), acute respiratory failure (trouble breathing), hypotension (low BP), and a decreased level of consciousness (less awake). A blood culture (test for germs in blood) grew staphylococcus aureus (type of bacteria) oxas (oxacillin) and you also had a coronavirus infection (COVID‑19) confirmed by rtPCR (viral test) on 03/15. You developed an acute kidney injury (kidney damage) classified as KDIGO 1 (mild) that was pre‑renal (due to low blood flow) but later resolved. Your liver cirrhosis (scarring of the liver) caused a pleural effusion (fluid around the lung) that needed both paracentesis (draining fluid from the abdomen) and thoracentesis (draining fluid from the chest) for relief.

On 09/19 you had a blood gas showing a pH of 1.61 (acid‑base measure), albumin 0.49 g/dL (low protein), serum albumin 2.1 g/dL, glucose 164 mg/dL, LDH 72 U/L (enzyme level), and serum LDH 314 U/L. A thoracentesis (chest fluid drain) on the same day showed transudate (thin fluid) with protein 2 g/dL, serum protein 7.7 g/dL, LDH 72 U/L, serum LDH 279 U/L, pH 7.378, albumin 0.61 g/dL, serum albumin 1.9 g/dL, amylase 117 U/L, glucose 183 mg/dL, and a negative culture (no germs). On 09/23/2022 you drained 700 ml of transudate, on 10/06/2022 you drained 1000 ml, on 10/10/2022 another 1000 ml, and on 10/15/2022 a further 1000 ml.

Your current illness began when [person] was diagnosed with liver cirrhosis of unclear cause, to be clarified later at the gastroclinic at [organization]. On 02/09/2022 you were advised to increase furosemide (diuretic to remove fluid) to 40 mg twice daily and spironolactone (potassium‑sparing diuretic) to 50 mg daily because of massive ascites (abdominal fluid), dyspnea (shortness of breath), and weight gain. A paracentesis (abdomen fluid drain) on that day removed 4.1 liters of fluid, and another on 13/09 removed 1.4 liters.

You were referred from the emergency unit with a report that you were admitted on 18/09/2022 with 85 % oxygen saturation on room air, obtunded (very sleepy), peripheral cyanosis (bluish skin) and livedo reticularis (mottled skin), and you were intubated (tube placed in airway) without problems. {omitted} noted that you developed dyspnea that morning. Four ampoules of furosemide were given but you produced no urine, according to the transport team. I admitted you intubated, sedated with midazolam (sleep‑inducing medicine) and fentanyl (pain medicine), paralyzed with rocuronium (muscle relaxant), and supported with norepinephrine (medicine to raise BP) at 20 ml/h.

Initially you were in {omitted}, where doctors thought your acute respiratory failure might be due to coronavirus, congestion, or lung infection (sepsis of pulmonary focus). Empirical ceftriaxone (antibiotic to fight infection) was started and a diagnostic paracentesis was done, which showed no spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (infection of abdominal fluid). On the same day a thoracentesis removed 1000 ml of transudate, and a relief paracentesis removed 4000 ml; albumin (protein given to keep fluid in vessels) was given because of the large fluid removal. A point‑of‑care ultrasound (pocus) on 09/19 showed lines and pleural thickening, supporting the lung infection theory.

Because the blood culture grew staphylococcus aureus, clarithromycin (antibiotic) and clindamycin (antibiotic) were added on 09/24, and the antibiotic regimen was changed from ceftriaxone + clarithromycin to levofloxacin (antibiotic) + oxacillin (antibiotic) as directed by the [organization]. An echocardiogram (heart ultrasound) was ordered to look for endocarditis (infection of heart lining) because of the bacteria in the blood. On the morning of 09/27, antibiotics were escalated to meropenem (strong antibiotic) + oxacillin because CRP (inflammation marker) rose and more vasoactive drugs were needed.

Your breathing improved, you were taken off the ventilator (extubated) on 10/03, and supplemental oxygen was stopped on 10/13. The septic condition resolved and the antibiotic course finished on 10/08. You stayed in the hospital because you needed 24‑hour nursing

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'. Keep explanations short (under 6-8 words per term).
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. CONCISENESS & LENGTH CONSTRAINT (CRITICAL): The simplified text must be concise and proportionate, strictly between 1.2x and 2.0x the word length of the original source report. Do NOT over-expand. Never list hypothetical normal ranges or unmentioned medical conditions. Only mention normal ranges for tests/vitals explicitly recorded in the document.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). 9. For each medication, state its name and brief purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic to fight infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (machine filtering waste when kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.

[person], a 60-year-old woman, was admitted on 09/19/2022 and discharged on 10/19/2022. She has a history of liver cirrhosis (scarring of the liver), diabetes (sugar), high BP, and anxiety/depression. She was admitted for septic shock (severe body-wide infection causing low BP), acute respiratory failure (breathing difficulty), and low consciousness. Blood tests found Staphylococcus aureus (a type of bacteria) and a prior coronavirus infection. She also had acute kidney injury (kidney stress) and fluid buildup in her belly (ascites) and chest (pleural effusion).

During her stay, she was intubated (breathing tube inserted) and sedated. Doctors performed paracentesis (draining belly fluid) and thoracentesis (draining chest fluid) multiple times to relieve pressure. Antibiotics were adjusted based on test results, including Ceftriaxone, Clarithromycin, Levofloxacin, Oxacillin, and Meropenem, to fight the infection. Her breathing improved, and the tube was removed on 10/03. She stayed in the hospital for nursing care, pressure injury treatment, and fluid management because she lacked social support at home.

Before admission, she took Insulin NPH and Glifage XR for sugar, Losartan and Hydrochlorothiazide for BP, Simvastatin for cholesterol, Sertraline and Amitriptyline for mood, Gabapentin for pain, Propranolol for heart protection, Omeprazole for stomach acid, and Furosemide/Spironolactone to reduce fluid. Her family was informed of her serious condition, and they decided together not to perform new invasive procedures. She was discharged with instructions to adjust diuretic doses, monitor kidney function, and continue fluid drainage as needed.

output_text:
Your mother, a 60-year-old woman, was admitted to the hospital on 19/09/2022 and discharged on 19/10/2022, staying for a total of 1 month and 11 hours. She was admitted due to liver cirrhosis (permanent scarring of the liver), which had led to several serious complications. At the time of admission, she was experiencing septic shock (a life-threatening drop in blood pressure caused by a severe infection), acute respiratory failure (difficulty breathing requiring machine support), and reduced consciousness (obtunded state). Her blood tests showed a blood infection caused by Staphylococcus Aureus bacteria. She also had acute kidney injury (temporary kidney damage), which has since resolved. Other conditions present included pleural effusion (fluid around the lungs), ascites (fluid buildup in the belly), diabetes mellitus (sugar disease), systemic arterial hypertension (high blood pressure), non-toxic multinodular goiter (enlarged thyroid gland), anxiety and depression, spondyloarthrosis (spine joint wear), and a fibroadenoma (a benign breast nodule).

When she first arrived, her oxygen saturation was critically low at 85% (normal range is 95-100%), her blood glucose was high at 164 mg/dL (normal range is 70-100 mg/dL), and her serum albumin was low at 2.1 g/dL (normal range is 3.5-5.0 g/dL). Her INR (a measure of how long it takes blood to clot) was critically high at 4.4 (normal range is 0.8-1.2), indicating a high risk of bleeding. Her LDH (a liver enzyme) was 72 U/L, which is within the normal range of 140-280 U/L, though this value is often monitored in liver disease. Her folic acid level was low at 1.29 ng/mL (normal range is 3.37 ng/mL). Imaging showed bilateral pleural effusion (fluid on both sides of the lungs) and cardiomegaly (an enlarged heart). She also developed pressure injuries (bedsores) during her stay.

To treat these issues, several procedures were performed. On 18/09/2022, she underwent orotracheal intubation (a tube placed in the windpipe to help her breathe). She was successfully extubated (the tube was removed) on 03/10/2022. On 19/09/2022, a paracentesis (a procedure to drain fluid from the belly) and a thoracentesis (a procedure to drain fluid from around the lungs) were performed. Additional thoracentesis procedures were carried out on 23/09/2022, 06/10/2022, 10/10/2022, and 15/10/2022 to remove accumulated fluid. A transthoracic echocardiography (an ultrasound of the heart) and a POCUS (Point of Care Ultrasound) were also performed on 19/09/2022 to assess her heart and fluid levels.

She received several medications to manage her conditions. For her sugar, she was given Insulin NPH (to control blood sugar) at a dosage noted as 1008, and Glifage XR (Metformin) to control blood sugar, taken as 2 tablets at lunch and 2 tablets at dinner. To lower her cholesterol, she took Simvastatin 20 mg daily. For her high blood pressure, she took Losartan 50 mg, 1 tablet every 12 hours, and Hydrochlorothiazide, a water pill to reduce fluid, once a day. For her mental health, she was prescribed Sertraline 50 mg, 1 tablet every 12 hours, for depression and anxiety. For nerve pain, she took Gabapentin 300 mg daily. For bone health, she received Calcium and Vitamin D. Amitriptyline 25 mg was given for pain or sleep. Propranolol 10 mg every 12 hours was prescribed to protect against bleeding in liver disease. Omeprazole 40 mg was given to reduce stomach acid. To reduce fluid in the belly and lungs, she took Furosemide 40 mg twice a day and Spironolactone 50 mg daily. Antibiotics were used to treat the infection: Levofloxacin was started on 23/09 and stopped on 26/09; Oxacillin was started on 24/09 and stopped on 08/10; and Meropenem, a strong antibiotic for severe infection, was started on 27/09 and stopped on 08/10.

Going forward, her treatment plan includes adjusting the doses of her water pills (diuretics) while closely monitoring her kidney function. She will continue to receive care for her pressure injuries and will gradually wean off oxygen therapy. You must watch for warning signs such as signs of infection (fever, chills), worsening shortness of breath, bleeding (vomiting blood or black stools), confusion or drowsiness, and significant weight gain or swelling. A follow-up appointment with the Gastroenterology department (AGAF) is scheduled for 18/01. The family has been informed about the severity of her condition and the prognosis, and a shared decision was made not to perform new invasive measures.

You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'. Keep explanations short (under 6-8 words per term).
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. CONCISENESS & LENGTH CONSTRAINT (CRITICAL): The simplified text must be concise and proportionate, strictly between 1.2x and 2.0x the word length of the original source report. Do NOT over-expand. Never list hypothetical normal ranges or unmentioned medical conditions. Only mention normal ranges for tests/vitals explicitly recorded in the document.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and brief purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic to fight infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (machine filtering waste when kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.

[person] was admitted to the hospital on 09/19/2022 and discharged on 10/19/2022, staying for 1 month and 11 hours in a ward. She is a 60-year-old female cleaner from [address] with incomplete high school education. Her estimated weight is 60 kg, predicted weight 57 kg, and height 164 cm. She has liver cirrhosis (scarring of the liver). During this stay, she had septic shock (severe infection causing low BP) from a lung source, acute respiratory failure (breathing difficulty), low BP, and decreased consciousness. Blood tests showed Staphylococcus aureus bacteria. She also had acute kidney injury (kidney stress) which resolved. Her liver condition caused pleural effusion (fluid around lungs) and ascites (fluid in belly), requiring paracentesis (draining belly fluid) and thoracentesis (draining lung fluid).

On 09/19, belly fluid tests showed low protein and albumin. Lung fluid tests showed it was a transudate (fluid from pressure, not infection). On 09/23, 700 ml of lung fluid was drained. On 10/06, 1000 ml was drained. On 10/10, 1000 ml was drained. On 10/15, 1000 ml was drained. Before this admission, she was seen on 02/09/2022 for massive ascites and breathing trouble. Her diuretics (water pills) were increased to Furosemide 40 mg twice daily and Spironolactone 50 mg daily. Paracentesis drained 4.1 liters that day. On 13/09, another paracentesis drained 1.4 liters. She was referred from emergency care on 18/09/2022 with low oxygen levels, confusion, and blue skin. She was intubated (breathing tube inserted) and sedated.

In the hospital, she was treated for possible lung infection or sepsis. Ceftriaxone (antibiotic) was started. Tests ruled out belly infection. Lung fluid was drained. A POCUS (quick ultrasound) showed lung lines and thickening, supporting sepsis. On 09/24, antibiotics changed to Levofloxacin and Oxacillin after blood cultures grew Staphylococcus aureus. An echocardiogram (heart ultrasound) was done to check for heart valve infection. On 09/27, antibiotics were escalated to Meropenem and Oxacillin due to worsening inflammation. She improved, was removed from the breathing tube on 10/03, and stopped oxygen on 10/13. Antibiotics ended on 10/08. She stayed longer for nursing care, pressure injury treatment, and fluid management.

Her history includes liver cirrhosis diagnosed in 2021, diabetes, high BP, and anxiety. She has had previous biopsies showing liver fibrosis and fatty liver. She has esophageal varices (swollen veins in food pipe). She is allergic to Dipyrone. She used to smoke and drink beer but stopped. Her home medicines include Insulin, Glifage XR (for sugar), Simvastatin (for cholesterol), Losartan (for BP), Hydrochlorothiazide (water pill), Sertraline (for mood), Gabapentin (for nerve pain), Calcium/Vitamin D, Amitriptyline (for pain/sleep), Propranolol (for BP/varices), Omeprazole (for stomach acid), Furosemide, and Spironolactone.

During the stay, she had a nasoenteral tube (feeding tube), central venous access (IV line in neck), and urinary catheter (urine tube). Blood cultures showed Staphylococcus aureus initially, then other harmless bacteria. Lung and belly fluid cultures were negative. A CT scan showed lung fluid and heart enlargement. The heart ultrasound showed normal pumping strength but some valve leakage.

At discharge, her diuretic doses will be adjusted while monitoring kidneys. She will continue to have belly and lung fluid drained as needed. Oxygen support will be reduced slowly. The feeding tube will be removed if she eats well. Pressure sores on her back and hips will be treated. She has a follow-up appointment on 18/01. The family has been informed about the seriousness of her condition. A decision was made together not to perform new invasive procedures.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'. Keep explanations short (under 6-8 words per term).
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.

Rules:

output_text:
You are a 60-year-old woman with liver cirrhosis (severe scarring of the liver). You were admitted on 09/19/2022 and discharged on 10/19/2022, staying for 1 month and 11 hours.

You were admitted from the emergency unit on 09/18/2022 because you had low oxygen levels (85% room air desaturation), were confused (obtunded), had bluish skin (peripheral cyanosis), and a mottled skin pattern (livedo reticularis). You were immediately put on a breathing tube (orotracheal intubation) without any problems. You had been feeling breathless since that morning. Before admission, you were given 4 injections of furosemide (a water pill) but did not pass any urine.

When you were admitted, you were on a breathing tube, sedated (given medicines to make you sleep) with midazolam and fentanyl, and given rocuronium (a muscle relaxant). Your blood pressure was stable with norepinephrine (a medicine to raise BP).

During your hospital stay, doctors thought you had acute respiratory failure (sudden lung failure) due to coronavirus, fluid buildup in the lungs (congestion), or a severe infection (sepsis) in your lungs. You had a coronavirus infection in March, confirmed by an RTPCR test on 03/15.

You were started on ceftriaxone (an antibiotic to fight infection). A paracentesis (procedure to drain fluid from the abdomen) was done, and there were no signs of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (an infection of the abdominal fluid). On the same day, a thoracentesis (procedure to drain fluid from around the lungs) was done, removing 1000 ml of fluid, which was a transudate (a type of fluid buildup). Another paracentesis was done, removing 4000 ml of fluid, and you were given albumin (a protein) because of the large fluid removal.

On 09/19, an ultrasound (POCUS) showed lines and thickening around your lungs, which, along with your breathing failure and need for BP-raising medicines, strongly suggested a lung infection (sepsis of pulmonary focus) as the cause of your breathing problems. So, clarithromycin and clindamycin (more antibiotics) were added.

On 09/24, after blood cultures (tests for infection in blood) showed growth of Staphylococcus aureus (a type of bacteria), your antibiotics were changed from ceftriaxone and clarithromycin to levofloxacin and oxacillin, as advised by [organization]. On the same day, an echocardiogram (heart ultrasound) was requested to check for endocarditis (infection of the heart valves) because of the bacteria found in your blood.

On 09/27 morning, your antibiotics were changed again to meropenem and oxacillin because your CRP (a marker of inflammation) worsened, and you needed more BP-raising medicines.

You slowly improved with your breathing and were taken off the breathing tube (extubation) on 10/03. Supplemental oxygen was stopped on 10/13. Your infection (septic condition) resolved, and you completed your antibiotic course on 10/08.

You remained in the hospital because you needed 24-hour nursing care, treatment for pressure injuries (bedsores), oxygen therapy, and management of ascites (fluid in the abdomen) and pleural effusion (fluid around the lungs). You did not have social support to go home.

You have a history of liver cirrhosis, first diagnosed in 2019, with the cause still being investigated. You have had complications like ascites, shp (hepatopulmonary syndrome, a lung problem due to liver disease) with medium-sized varices (swollen veins), spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, eh (hepatic encephalopathy, brain dysfunction due to liver disease), and upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

You also have a history of diabetes (sugar) for 15 years, hypertension (high BP) for 10 years, and a non-toxic multinodular goiter (swelling in the thyroid gland) diagnosed in 2019. You have anxiety and depression, diagnosed 6 years ago, and spondyloarthrosis (arthritis of the spine) with low back pain. You have a painful lump in your right breast, which was biopsied in November 2019 and was likely a fibroadenoma (a non-cancerous lump).

You used to smoke one pack a day for a few months and drank 3-4 cans of beer on weekends but stopped 2 years ago. You deny using illicit drugs.

Before this hospitalization, you were taking several medications: Insulin NPH (for sugar), Glifage XR 500 mg (for sugar), Simvastatin 20 mg/day (for cholesterol), Losartan 50 mg (for BP), Hydrochlorothiazide (a water pill), Sertraline 50 mg (for depression), Gabapentin 300 mg/day (for nerve pain), Calcium and vitamin D, Amitriptyline 25 mg (for depression/nerve pain), Propranolol 10 mg (for BP and varices), Omeprazole 40 mg (for acidity), Furosemide 40 mg twice a day (a water pill), and Spironolactone 50 mg/d (a water pill).

On 02/09/2022, you had a consultation where your furosemide was increased to 40 mg twice daily and spironolactone to 50 mg/d due to massive ascites (a lot of fluid in the abdomen), dyspnea (breathlessness), and weight gain. A paracentesis was done, draining 4.1 liters of fluid. Another paracentesis was done on 09/13, draining 1.4 liters.

During this admission, you had several thoracentesis procedures: on 09/19, 09/23 (drained 700 ml), 10/06 (drained 1000 ml), 10/10 (drained 1000 ml), and 10/15 (drained 1000 ml). The fluid was a transudate, and cultures were negative.

Blood cultures showed Staphylococcus aureus on 09/19, Staphylococcus epidermidis on 09/24, and Staphylococcus capitis on 09/28. All were resistant to oxacillin. Urine, pleural fluid, ascitic fluid, and catheter tip cultures were negative.

A CT scan on 09/21 showed bilateral pulmonary opacities (shadows in both lungs) that could be fluid or inflammation, bilateral pleural effusion (fluid around both lungs) with atelectasis (collapsed lung areas) in the lower parts, and cardiomegaly (enlarged heart). An echocardiogram showed a normal ejection fraction (heart's pumping strength) of 59%, a dilated left atrium (upper heart chamber), preserved ventricular systolic performance (normal squeezing of the main pumping chambers), normal heart wall movement, mild mitral and tricuspid valve insufficiency (mild leakage of heart valves), and mild left ventricular diastolic dysfunction (mild problem with heart relaxing).

Your plan for discharge includes adjusting your water pill doses, closely watching your kidney function, continuing relief paracentesis and thoracentesis as needed, gradually reducing oxygen therapy, assessing if the feeding tube (nasoenteric tube) can be removed if you eat well by mouth, and caring for your pressure injuries on your back and hips. You have a follow-up appointment at AGAF on 01/18. Your family has been informed about the seriousness of your condition and the possible outcomes, and a shared decision was made not to perform any new invasive procedures.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'.
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.

The tissue that was taken out during the prostate surgery was the prostate gland itself. The surgeon removed a piece that weighed 50 grams and measured 5.1 × 4.3 × 3.2 centimeters. The specimen also included the seminal vesicles (the glands that produce part of the fluid in semen) and the ductus deferentes (the tubes that carry sperm).

When the pathologist examined the tissue under a microscope, they found acinar adenocarcinoma (a cancer that starts in the gland cells of an organ) that was present on both sides of the prostate (bilateral). The cancer was coded with the ICD‑O‑3 number 8140/3.

The cancer cells were graded using the Gleason system. The score is 4 + 3 = 7 (7b). The first number (4) is the most common pattern of the cancer cells, the second number (3) is the second most common pattern. A score of 7 means the cells look moderately abnormal and the cancer is moderately aggressive. The ISUP Grade Group is 3, which is the same level of seriousness. Sixty percent of the tumor cells were the high‑grade pattern (pattern 4) and forty percent were the lower‑grade pattern (pattern 3).

The cancer had grown into the sheaths that surround nerves (perineural invasion: present). It had not spread into the seminal vesicles (Seminal vesicle invasion: absent).

The surgeon removed all of the visible cancer, and the edges of the removed tissue (resection margins) were clear. The apical margin (the top edge) was negative, the basal margin (the bottom edge) was negative, and the sedimentation lines (the lines where the tissue was cut) were negative. Because all margins are clear, the resection status is R0, meaning no cancer cells were found at the edges.

The remaining prostate tissue still contains a benign condition called adenomyomatosis (a thickening of the prostate gland walls). The pathologist will do additional examinations to confirm the findings and will report back.

You had a detailed brain and ear scan called an MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging), which uses strong magnets and radio waves to take pictures of your body without using any radiation. This specific scan looked at your brain and the bones around your ears and face. To get clearer pictures, a special dye called contrast was given through an IV. The scan used several different types of image settings, including T1-weighted, FLAIR, T2-weighted, SWI, DWI, and CISS sequences, to look at different parts of the tissue in detail. The reason for this test was to check for the cause of pain in your left face and jaw, as well as the weakness in your left facial muscles that started one month ago.

First, it is good news that many important parts of your head are healthy. The brainstem (the part of the brain that connects to the spinal cord and controls basic life functions), the cerebellum (the part of the brain that controls balance and coordination), and the main brain tissue (cerebral parenchyma) all look normal. The fluid-filled spaces in the brain called ventricles and the grooves on the surface of the brain called sulci are also normal. The special image sequences (DWI, SWI, and post-contrast sections) inside the skull did not show any specific problems. The part of the left facial nerve that comes out of the brain (the postganglionic segment) is normal, as is the section of the nerve in the fluid-filled space around the brain (the cisternal segment). The bones of your skull, other than the specific spots mentioned below, are normal. In the ear area, both middle ears and the air-filled spaces in the mastoid bone (the bony area behind the ears) are clear, and the inner ear structures are normal.

There are a few areas that need attention. In the bone next to the opening where the jugular vein enters the skull (the left jugular foramen) and near the vertical part of the left facial nerve, there is a small, solid spot in the bone. This spot does not take up the contrast dye, which is a good sign. It is slightly expanded, meaning it has pushed the bone out a tiny bit, but it is the same size as it was in your previous MRI records from the e-Nabız system, so it is stable and likely an old, chronic finding. Because it does not light up with the dye, it makes it less likely to be certain types of tumors like glomus jugulare or lymphoma. However, doctors still need to check if this is related to any serious disease that affects the bone marrow.

Additionally, there are similar spots in the bone marrow of the parietal bones (the bones on the top and sides of your skull) on both the left and right sides. Two of these spots at the very top of your head (the vertex) show a reaction in the outer layer of the bone called periosteal reaction, which means the outer bone layer is reacting to something underneath. These findings are not fully explained yet, so they are considered indeterminate.

Regarding your facial weakness, there is mild swelling and dye uptake in the part of the left facial nerve before it enters the ear (the preganglionic segment). This is consistent with Bell's palsy, which is a common condition that causes temporary weakness in the facial muscles. The radiologist’s overall impression is that there is no disease inside the brain itself. The bone spots are likely not dangerous tumors like glomus jugulare or lymphoma because they don't enhance with dye, but they do require further evaluation to rule out any malignant diseases that might involve the bone marrow.

To make sure everything is safe, two follow-up actions are recommended. First, you should have a CT scan of the temporal bones (the bones around the ears) as a routine next step. This will help doctors see the tiny internal structure of the bone, known as bone trabeculation, more clearly. Second, and more urgently, you need to be evaluated for any malignant diseases that could be causing these bone marrow changes. This is important to rule out any serious conditions given the presence of multiple bone spots with the outer bone reaction.

The bones of your skull, your eyes, the fat behind your eyes, and the optic nerves (the cables that carry vision from your eyes to your brain) are all normal. The main blood vessels in your brain are open and working correctly. There is some thickening of the lining in the maxillary sinuses (behind your cheeks), ethmoid cells (between your eyes), and frontal sinuses (above your eyebrows), which suggests a sinus infection or inflammation.
